_note: Corridor geometry, illustrative habitat zones and crossing concepts for WildPass. Keys match the region ids in regions.json. See data_notes for what is and is not verified.

data_notes.roads: Approximate highway alignments traced from OpenStreetMap data (copyright OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL) via the OSRM routing service on 2026-10-16 and simplified. Not surveyed centerlines.
data_notes.habitats: Illustrative circular habitat zones placed near known wildlife areas for demonstration. Not mapped habitat or corridor boundaries.
data_notes.solutions: General crossing-structure types matched to animal groups. Concepts only; real projects need ecological surveys, collision records and engineering review.
data_notes.priority: Priority combines daily vehicle-km through each habitat zone (road length inside the zone times Caltrans annual average daily traffic at the nearest count point) with legal protection status: High at 200,000+ vehicle-km/day or when a listed species is present, Medium at 75,000+, otherwise Low. It ranks where to look first; it is not measured collision risk.
data_notes.overlays: Proposed crossing points are concepts, not surveyed sites. I-15's Santa Rosa Plateau circle, obstruction zone and blocked-movement arrows are the frontend team's hand-drawn illustrations; the arrow ends were moved onto the OpenStreetMap road.

causeway.name: Elevated causeway segment
causeway.description: Raise the road on a causeway over the marsh so tidal flow and wetland habitat reconnect beneath it and wildlife stays off the roadway.

overpass.name: Vegetated wildlife overpass
overpass.description: A landscaped bridge over the highway that large mammals can cross on natural ground.

underpass.name: Wildlife undercrossing or enlarged culvert
underpass.description: A wide, open passage under the road, such as a bridge span or box culvert, for mid-sized mammals.

small_culvert.name: Small-animal culverts with cover
small_culvert.description: Small, dry culverts with vegetation or cover at the entrances so small mammals can pass under the road.

dry_ledge.name: Waterway crossing with dry banks or ledges
dry_ledge.description: Bridges or culverts at creeks and sloughs that keep a dry path under the road, so otters do not climb onto the highway.

fencing.name: Directional fencing
fencing.description: Fencing along the highway that keeps animals off the road and guides them toward the crossing structure.

hand_drawn._note: The frontend team's I-15 map design (frontend/src/data/fallback.js), served by the API so all three regions come from the backend. Shapes are illustrative; every card claim is backed by this corridor's sources.

cards.title: Species of concern
cards.subtext: Mountain lion (Santa Ana Mountains population, threatened under the California Endangered Species Act since February 2026), southern mule deer and bobcat: all focal species of the 2023 I-15 wildlife crossing design report

cards.title: I-15 barrier effect
cards.subtext: Caltrans count nearest the Temecula Creek conflict; 150,000 near Rainbow Canyon and 142,500 to 198,000 across the 7 count points from Rainbow to Temecula (retrieved 2026-10-16). A busy 10-lane freeway (UC Davis, 2014).

cards.title: Genetic fragmentation
cards.subtext: A nearly impermeable barrier to puma movement, resulting in severe genetic restriction (Vickers et al. 2015); Santa Ana Mountains lions have lower genetic diversity than those in nearly every other region of California (Ernest et al. 2014)

cards.title: Collision mortality
cards.subtext: Mountain lions killed on California roads, 2015 to 2022; I-15 south of Temecula is named among the problem highways (UC Davis Road Ecology Center)

cards.title: Verified mortality corridor
cards.subtext: Unmarked mountain lions found dead on the I-15 freeway, 2001 to 2013; vehicle collisions caused 28% of deaths among radio-collared pumas (Vickers et al. 2015, PLOS ONE)

cards.title: Planned crossings
cards.subtext: The Nature Conservancy and Caltrans are developing an enhanced Temecula Creek Bridge, a new vegetated wildlife overcrossing and a wildlife culvert on a 3-mile stretch of I-15 (design report, 2023)

sd-i15.name: San Diego County: Interstate 15 Corridor (Temecula / Rainbow Canyon)

sources.title: A highway runs through it: Mountain lions in southern California face genetic decay
sources.publisher: UC Davis, on Ernest et al. (PLOS ONE)
sources.supports: I-15, a busy 10-lane highway, bisects the small habitat linkage between Santa Ana Mountains mountain lions and the Peninsular Ranges; pumas in the Santa Ana Mountains showed lower genetic diversity than those from nearly every other region in the state.

sources.title: A lion tale: Humans cause most mountain lion deaths in Southern California
sources.publisher: UC Davis, on Vickers et al. (PLOS ONE)
sources.supports: Humans directly caused more than half of known mountain lion deaths, including vehicle collisions; annual survival was about 56%; I-15 is nearly impossible for lions to cross.

sources.title: Mountain Lion Listed as Threatened Species in Central and Southern California under the California Endangered Species Act
sources.publisher: Allen Matkins legal alert, on the California Fish and Game Commission decision
sources.supports: On February 12, 2026 the Commission listed the Southern California / Central Coast mountain lion population, which includes the Santa Ana Mountains and Eastern Peninsular Range, as threatened.

sources.title: Traffic Volumes: Annual Average Daily Traffic (AADT)
sources.supports: Daily traffic at count points along the corridor, used to estimate how many vehicle-kilometres pass through each habitat zone every day.

sources.title: Survival and Mortality of Pumas (Puma concolor) in a Fragmented, Urbanizing Landscape
sources.supports: I-15 and associated development have created a nearly impermeable barrier to puma movements, resulting in severe genetic restriction; vehicle collisions caused 28% of deaths of radio-collared pumas (2001 to 2013), and six unmarked pumas were found dead on the I-15 freeway.

sources.title: Mountain Lion Mortality Maps Show Rough Road for Cougars
sources.supports: One or two mountain lions were killed every week on California roads and highways between 2015 and 2022; I-15 south of Temecula is listed among the problem highways.

sources.title: Interstate 15 Wildlife Crossings: Design Considerations for Focal Wildlife Species (Santa Ana-Palomar Mountains Linkage)
sources.publisher: The Nature Conservancy, Caltrans, U.S. Geological Survey, UC Davis Wildlife Health Center, San Diego State University and others
sources.supports: Three wildlife crossing projects are being developed on a 3-mile stretch of I-15: enhancement of the existing Temecula Creek Bridge, a new vegetated wildlife overcrossing (spanning 10 lanes of highway) and a new wildlife culvert. Focal species include mountain lion, southern mule deer and bobcat.

San Diego/Riverside County Line (SD postmile R54.258)

mountain_lion.label: Threatened under the California Endangered Species Act (Southern California / Central Coast population, listed February 2026)

mortality.summary: 6 unmarked mountain lions found dead on the I-15 freeway, 2001 to 2013; vehicle collisions caused 28% of deaths among radio-collared pumas.

cv-sr152.name: Central Valley / South Bay: Highway 152 (Pacheco Pass / San Luis Reservoir)
cv-sr152.species_note: Recorded on SR-152 by the Pathways for Wildlife 2021-2022 camera and roadkill study (7,554 wildlife passages at 23 culverts and 6 bridges; 42 animals hit; an adult male tule elk killed on 2022-02-17). Black Bear is a hackathon prompt species for this region but was not recorded in that study, so it is not used in the analysis.
cv-sr152.plan_note: Official plan: the Pacheco Pass Wildlife Connectivity Project proposes up to 3 wildlife crossings (2 overcrossings, 1 undercrossing) and up to 10 miles of directional fencing on SR-152 (CEQAnet 2025100438).

sources.title: SR-152 Pacheco Pass Regional Wildlife Connectivity Study 2021-2022
sources.publisher: Pathways for Wildlife, for the California Department of Fish and Wildlife and the Santa Clara Valley Habitat Agency
sources.supports: SR-152 bisects the Diablo Range to Inner Coast Linkage and the State Wildlife Action Plan lists it as a priority for a tule elk overpass. Cameras at 23 culverts and 6 bridges recorded 7,554 wildlife passages (coyote, mule deer, bobcat, mountain lion and tule elk among them; black bear is not mentioned); 42 animals were recorded hit by vehicles in June 2021 to June 2022, and an adult male tule elk was hit near San Luis Reservoir in February 2022.

sources.title: Pacheco Pass Wildlife Connectivity Project (Notice of Exemption)
sources.publisher: Santa Clara Valley Habitat Agency, via CEQAnet
sources.supports: Proposes up to three wildlife crossing structures on SR-152 between postmiles 27.5 and 34.6 (two girder-bridge overcrossings, one tunnel undercrossing) and up to 10 miles of directional fencing, for elk, mule deer, mountain lions and other mesocarnivores.

sources.title: Traffic Volumes: Annual Average Daily Traffic (AADT)
sources.supports: Daily traffic at count points along the corridor, used to estimate how many vehicle-kilometres pass through each habitat zone every day.

Santa Clara/Merced County Line (MER postmile R0)

mortality.summary: 42 animals recorded hit by vehicles on SR-152, June 2021 to June 2022: striped skunk 10, coyote 9, deer 8, bobcat 6, raccoon 5, mountain lion 1 and 3 others.

sites.label: Adult male tule elk hit by a vehicle, 2022-02-17

nb-sr37.name: Northern California / North Bay: State Route 37 (San Pablo Baylands Corridor)
nb-sr37.plan_note: Official plan: the state's preferred long-term design for SR-37 is a fully elevated causeway that restores the tidal connection between the Bay and the baylands (California Natural Resources Agency).

sources.title: State and Local Agencies Announce Commitments to Create a Climate-Resilient Highway 37
sources.supports: The preferred long-term alternative is a fully elevated causeway that restores the hydrological connection between the Bay and the baylands; restored wetlands provide habitat for endangered species including the salt marsh harvest mouse.

sources.title: Salt-marsh Harvest Mouse (Reithrodontomys raviventris)
sources.supports: Endangered species; the northern subspecies lives in the marshes of San Pablo and Suisun bays, where its distribution follows pickleweed.

sources.title: Salt Marsh Harvest Mouse (Reithrodontomys raviventris) fact sheet
sources.supports: Status: federal endangered; California endangered.

sources.title: State Route 37: Sears Point to Mare Island Improvement Project
sources.supports: SR 37 narrows to one lane in each direction between SR 121 and the Mare Island interchange; the project would replace the Tolay Creek Bridge and widen the Sonoma Creek Bridge.

sources.title: Traffic Volumes: Annual Average Daily Traffic (AADT)
sources.supports: Daily traffic at count points along the corridor, used to estimate how many vehicle-kilometres pass through each habitat zone every day.

sources.title: Enhancing Community and Wildlife Resilience to Sea-Level Rise and Infrastructure Development in the San Pablo Baylands
sources.supports: State Route 37 is dubbed the Flyway Highway for its route through miles of waterbird habitat; the baylands support over half a million migratory birds a year and the salt marsh harvest mouse.

sources.title: San Pablo Bay National Wildlife Refuge Bird Checklist
sources.publisher: Friends of San Pablo Bay NWR
sources.supports: Northern harrier (marsh hawk) is listed as common in every season, alongside many species of ducks and other waterfowl.

sources.title: River Otters Are Thriving All Over the Bay Area
sources.supports: The River Otter Ecology Project reports many river otter sightings in Sonoma, Napa and Marin.

us101-redwood.name: North Coast: US-101 Redwood Coastal Corridor (Stone Lagoon / Orick)
us101-redwood.plan_note: Official plan: Caltrans and CDFW will install an elk detection system on PM 114.0-115.5 near Stone Lagoon (Coastal Commission permit 1-23-0909): 25 transceivers, 2 changeable message signs and 4 flashing elk warning signs; the study runs to December 2027. This stretch was ranked the top priority in Caltrans District 1 for large-mammal roadkill (Western Transportation Institute, 2019).

sources.title: Coastal Development Permit 1-23-0909 (Caltrans Elk Detection System), staff report
sources.supports: Elk detection system on a 1.6-mile stretch of US-101 near Stone Lagoon (PM 114.0 to 115.5): 25 transceivers on 8-foot posts, two 10-foot changeable message signs, four elk warning signs with flashing beacons, up to three speed recorders. Resident herd of about 77 elk. Highest concentration of elk crossings in coastal Humboldt and Del Norte counties; ranked highest priority in Caltrans District 1 (Huijser and Begley, 2019).

sources.title: Stone Lagoon U.S. 101 Elk Electronic Detection System (Research Notes, Task 4054)
sources.publisher: Caltrans Division of Research, Innovation and System Information
sources.supports: Caltrans and CDFW will install the system on about one mile of US-101 near Stone Lagoon; task runs April 2023 to December 2027. Roosevelt elk vehicle collisions have increased dramatically in the past 20 years; the highway bisects elk corridors between coastal forest, prairie, lagoon and marsh habitats.
